name: Scientific racism
summary: Scientific racism is the belief, dressed as science, that humanity divides into biologically distinct races whose inherited traits justify ranking them and treating them differently. Its classic texts (Gobineau, Grant) make race the key to history, warn that race mixture and immigration doom a people, and call for restriction of entry, eugenic breeding and rule by the best-bred. Modern science rejects its central claims.
scope: The classic tradition as the reference works describe it: Gobineau's Essay on the Inequality of the Human Races (1853-55), the American strand of Madison Grant (The Passing of the Great Race, 1916), and the eugenics of Francis Galton as the encyclopedias tie it to racial theory. The later 'human biodiversity' current is named by Wikipedia but its own texts are not used here, and no answer rests on it. Positions of regimes or parties that used the claims (Nazi Germany, apartheid) are other subjects.

notes: Searched the local Gutenberg texts of Grant, Gobineau, Stoddard and Galton, and the Wikipedia and Encyclopedia.com articles, for every theme (economy, government, society, world, liberty, culture, ecology, technology, means). The classic texts are about race, heredity, immigration, eugenics and rule by the best-bred; they say nothing on most economic, constitutional or ecological questions, which stay null. The modern human-biodiversity current is named by Wikipedia but has no texts here, so earlier answers resting on it were nulled. Earlier answers that guessed what adherents would think (including 0 'splits' with no evidence on each side) were nulled. The record leaves the Secularism / Theocracy line (religion appears only as Gobineau's claim that Christianity neither creates nor changes a race's capacity for civilization, and Grant's remarks on the Church) and the foreign-policy and economy lines thinly covered; the uncertainty rule rejects the profile on that evidence, which is an honest result.

keyFigures.role: Author of the Essay on the Inequality of the Human Races (1853)
keyFigures.quote: His name was Count Arthur de Gobineau (1816–1882)

keyFigures.role: Author of The Passing of the Great Race (1916), promoter of Nordic race theory and immigration restriction
keyFigures.quote: a Yale-educated lawyer and amateur naturalist named Madison Grant, syncretized Davenport’s genetics with Gobineau’s racism

keyFigures.role: Founder of eugenics and of the statistical study of inherited intelligence
keyFigures.quote: Galton called for the scientific control of human breeding
